tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — OPEN PANICLE + SHEATH
tiles.details: Start with the existing source-labelled in-ground habit photograph (panel 3), the genuine collected fibrous-rooted crown (panel 5), and an open pyramidal flowering head (USFS reports culms about 30–90 cm, panicles about 15–35 cm). Follow the same stem down to its sheath: plains lovegrass is often relatively smooth on the sheath body, with hairs concentrated near the throat; occasional sheath hairs and bearded lower branch axils occur, so 'hairless' is not an absolute rule. Purple hue or a cloudlike head alone is not a species diagnosis.
tiles.short: Fine, widely spreading perennial panicle; inspect mostly smooth sheath BODY before deciding.
tiles.status: ROOTED CROWN AND HABIT PHOTOS AVAILABLE — SAME-PLANT TEXAS FLOWERING VOUCHER NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE, NOT OUTER HAIRS
tiles.details: Open a mature blade at its INNER blade–sheath junction and photograph at 10–20× with a 1-mm scale. Go Botany describes a 0.2–0.4 mm hair-fringed or membranous-ciliate ligule. The conspicuous hairs behind the throat are separate; do not draw a ligule arrow on a distant sheath photograph. Compare hair distribution on at least two sheaths from the same plant. Bob Harms' existing panel 4 shows the authentic collar/sheath region and a source scale, but does NOT independently isolate the free inner 0.2–0.4 mm ligule.
tiles.short: Inner ligule only about 0.2–0.4 mm; outer collar/throat hairs may be much longer.
tiles.status: SCALED EXTERIOR COLLAR AVAILABLE — TRUE INNER LIGULE STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 03 · TRACE PANICLE BRANCHES AND PEDICELS
tiles.details: Find a complete mature panicle and photograph the lower branch junctions and several attached spikelet pedicels. USFS describes a diffuse pyramidal panicle; published pedicel-to-spikelet length and floret counts conflict between Texas A&M and UT/FNA-related treatments. Do NOT use a single rigid pedicel-ratio cutoff, and do not treat a few axillary hairs as proof of bigtop lovegrass.
tiles.short: Open 15–35 cm panicle; tiny spikelets on delicate divergent stalks.
tiles.status: OPEN PANICLE PHOTOS AVAILABLE — LOWER AXIL AND PEDICEL SCALE NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE A MATURE MULTIFLORETED SPIKELET
tiles.details: Isolate two or three fully mature, laterally compressed spikelets with a physical millimeter rule; Go Botany reports 3–7 mm and more than one floret, while the historical Texas treatment reports 2–9 florets and 3–10 mm. Count individual overlapping florets, not panicle branches. Treat published variation as a source-concept comparison, not an unverified measurement of archived photographs. Bob Harms' existing panel 6 already shows source-identified mature spikelets with a millimeter scale; do not request another generic spikelet view. Remaining work is to verify floret counts and any conflicting measurement ranges on attached material.
tiles.short: Spikelets about 3–7 mm in Go Botany; broader 3–10 mm reported in a Texas treatment.
tiles.status: SCALED MATURE SPIKELETS AVAILABLE — FLORET COUNT / SOURCE CONCEPT QA

tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE BOTH GLUMES AND AN AWNLESS LEMMA
tiles.details: Published Go Botany gives upper glume 1.3–2 mm, lemma 1.8–2.2 mm and a 0-mm lemma awn; a historical Texas description reports lower glume ~1–1.2 mm and lemma ~1.8–2.5 mm. At 20–40× dissect the basal pair of one-veined glumes and a mature three-veined fertile lemma/palea. Do not confuse the upper glume with the first lemma or fabricate glume-nerve arrows on a whole-head photograph. Bob Harms' panel 7 already shows a real separated lemma, palea and grain with source scale. Do not call all dissection anatomy missing: specifically resolve lower/upper glume attachment and individual vein counts at suitable magnification.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~1–1.2 mm, upper ~1.3–2 mm; lemma ~1.8–2.2 mm, 3-veined and AWNLESS.
tiles.status: REAL SCALED LEMMA/PALEA DISSECTION AVAILABLE — GLUME/VEIN MACRO GAP

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC GATE
tiles.details: E. hirsuta often has conspicuous hairs across the sheath BODY and bearded panicle axils; E. trichodes is usually taller with longer hairs concentrated at the sheath THROAT and a large oblong head. E. spectabilis makes a broad, often tumbling flowering cloud. Color, a single hairy axil and a single airy photograph are not decisive. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same authenticated Central Texas plant linking the rooted crown to a mature head; opened and measured inner ligule; lower branch axils; separate glume bases and lemma veins if not resolved by existing scaled Bob Harms panels. Existing panels 5–7 already document real roots, scaled spikelets and separated lemma/palea. NEEDS_SITE_QA: review ten current panels, ten image records, ten existing markers, original licenses including CC BY-NC exclusions where applicable, identity/attribution, all arrow endpoints, and public mobile rendering. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Plains vs bigtop vs sand: inspect WHERE sheath hairs grow, then measure spikelets.
tiles.status: DIFFERENT-SPECIES COMPARISONS 8–9 VERIFIED IN CARD — MATCHED SHEATH MACROS / SITE QA NEEDED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: PLAINS LOVEGRASS: real source-labelled photographs show a fine, OPEN delicate panicle of tiny dark spikelets and a true basal tussock in dry rocky ground. Typical mature sheath BODY is relatively smooth, with hairs more concentrated at throat/collar; lower panicle axils can ALSO bear hairs, so one tuft is not decisive. Compare bigtop hirsute sheaths and taller sand lovegrass; confirm collar and measured ripe spikelets for difficult specimens.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Photograph an intact open mature head and its small, distinct spikelets (the existing photo arrows teach this only).
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Start with the existing source-labelled in-ground habit photograph (panel 3), the genuine collected fibrous-rooted crown (panel 5), and an open pyramidal flowering head (USFS reports culms about 30–90 cm, panicles about 15–35 cm). Follow the same stem down to its sheath: plains lovegrass is often relatively smooth on the sheath body, with hairs concentrated near the throat; occasional sheath hairs and bearded lower branch axils occur, so 'hairless' is not an absolute rule. Purple hue or a cloudlike head alone is not a species diagnosis.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Start with the existing source-labelled in-ground habit photograph (panel 3), the genuine collected fibrous-rooted crown (panel 5), and an open pyramidal flowering head (USFS reports culms about 30–90 cm, panicles about 15–35 cm). Follow the same stem down to its sheath: plains lovegrass is often relatively smooth on the sheath body, with hairs concentrated near the throat; occasional sheath hairs and bearded lower branch axils occur, so 'hairless' is not an absolute rule. Purple hue or a cloudlike head alone is not a species diagnosis.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: E. hirsuta usually has more conspicuous hairs on the sheath surface/margins and bearded panicle axils; E. trichodes commonly has a taller, elongated diffuse panicle and long hairs concentrated at the sheath throat, with spikelets sometimes near branch tips. E. spectabilis can make an exceptionally broad loose purple tumbleweed-like panicle. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) has a different spikelet construction; dissect before using color or openness.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.
